options: How you split money between shares, bonds and cash
Choosing which single share to buy
questions.why: It's the split between asset types, and it drives most of a portfolio's risk and expected return.

questions.q: You start with £6,000 in shares and £4,000 in bonds (60/40). Shares rise {s} and bonds don't change. What % of the pot is now in shares? (One decimal place.)
questions.why: Shares become £6,000 × (1 + {s}); divided by the new total gives {answer}%. Your risk has drifted above 60%.

questions.q: Your 60/40 portfolio has drifted to 68/32 after a strong year for shares. What does rebalancing involve?
options: Selling some shares and buying bonds to get back to 60/40
Buying more shares because they're doing well
questions.why: Rebalancing sells what grew and buys what lagged, returning risk to the level you chose.

questions.q: Match each goal to a mix that could suit it.
pairs: Goal in 8 years, nervous of falls
Balanced mix of shares and bonds
questions.why: Short timeframes need cash; long ones can take more in shares; nerves matter too.

questions.q: Holding ten different global index funds is much more diversified than holding one.
questions.why: They'd largely hold the same companies. One broad fund already holds thousands; more funds add cost and complexity, not diversification.

questions.q: Put these homes for long-term investing in the usual order of priority for an employee.
items: Workplace pension up to the employer match
questions.why: Take free employer money and tax relief first, then tax-free ISAs, then taxable accounts.

questions.q: The news predicts a market crash. Your allocation fits your 30-year goal. What does your plan usually say to do?
options: Nothing different: the allocation already expects falls
Move everything into the predicted winners
questions.why: Crash forecasts are often wrong and badly timed. Acting on them is recency bias and herding.

questions.q: Assume shares return 5% a year above inflation, bonds 1.5% and cash 0.5%. What's the expected return of a {s}% shares, {b}% bonds, rest cash portfolio, in %?
questions.why: Weight each return by its share of the pot and add up: {answer}% a year (under these assumptions).

questions.q: What does a multi-asset (e.g. 60/40) fund do for you?
options: Holds shares and bonds in a set mix and rebalances automatically
Picks the best shares each week
questions.why: It's an all-in-one fund: one decision, automatic rebalancing. It can still fall and still charges fees.

questions.q: Explain the three things that should decide how much of your portfolio goes into shares.

ideas.label: Timeframe: when you'll need the money
Need: how much growth the goal requires
Nerve: how you'd really behave in a fall

questions.model: Timeframe (money needed within about five years shouldn't be in shares), need (how much growth the goal actually requires, so you don't take more risk than necessary), and nerve (how you'd really behave in a crash, because a portfolio you abandon is worse than a duller one you keep).
questions.why: Allocation should fit the goal and the person.

tests.answer: How long until I need the money, what return my goal needs, and how I'd react to a crash.
How many years I'm investing for.
Which shares are popular right now.

questions.q: Explain two benefits of rebalancing a portfolio once a year.

ideas.label: Keeps your risk at the level you chose
Makes you sell high and buy low by rule, not emotion

questions.model: It keeps your risk at the level you chose instead of drifting higher after good years. And it makes you sell some of what's risen and buy what's fallen by rule, which means buying low and selling high without relying on emotion.
questions.why: Rebalancing is risk control plus built-in discipline.

tests.answer: It brings the risk back to my target and makes me sell high and buy low by rule.
It stops your portfolio drifting from the target.
